From brms to bmm

Gidon Frischkorn

Ven Popov

Source: vignettes/articles/bmm_brms_to_bmm.Rmd
bmm_brms_to_bmm.Rmd

1 Who this article is for

You know brms. You have written brm(y ~ x + (1 | id)), read its summary, and perhaps written a non-linear formula or two. Then you open a bmm article and the formula has no response on its left-hand side, the model is an object of its own, and the estimates come with links you did not choose. This article translates between the two packages.

We fit one model twice: once in plain brms, once with bmm. The model is the two-parameter mixture model for continuous reproduction tasks (Zhang and Luck 2008), which brms can express with its built-in mixture family. Both fits run the same Stan model, so they give the same estimates. With that established, the rest of the article explains each difference in the code: where the response went, why every parameter gets its own formula, what 0 + setsize and 1 + setsize each give you, which scale the estimates are on, and why bmm sets informative default priors. A later section does the same comparison for signal detection: trial-level sdt_yn() against a probit generalized linear mixed model.

2 The same model, written twice

2.1 The data

zhang_luck_2008 ships with bmm. Eight participants saw one, two, three or six colored squares, and after a delay they reproduced the color of one of them on a color wheel. The response error is the distance between the reported and the true color, in radians:

library(bmm)
library(brms)

dat <- zhang_luck_2008
head(dat[, c("subID", "setsize", "response_error")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   subID setsize response_error
#>   <dbl> <fct>            <dbl>
#> 1     1 6              -1.85  
#> 2     1 1              -0.0698
#> 3     1 2              -0.0349
#> 4     1 2               0.0349
#> 5     1 6              -1.54  
#> 6     1 3               0.733

setsize is a factor. With a numeric column, 0 + setsize below would fit a single slope instead of one value per set size.

The mixture model assumes that a response comes either from memory or from a guess. Memory responses scatter around the true color with a von Mises distribution, the normal distribution of the circle, whose precision is kappa. Guesses fall anywhere on the circle with equal probability. The second parameter is the probability that a response comes from memory. We let both parameters differ between set sizes and between participants.

2.2 The model in brms

In brms, this is a mixture of two von Mises distributions. Each component has a location (mu1, mu2) and a precision (kappa1, kappa2), and theta1 is the weight of the first component. Turning this into the mixture model takes three constraints. Both locations are fixed at 0, because the response error is already relative to the target. The precision of the second component is fixed at a value so small that the distribution is flat, which makes it the guessing distribution. Constant priors do the fixing:

brms_fit <- brm(
  formula = bf(
    response_error ~ 1,
    kappa1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    theta1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    mu2 ~ 1,
    kappa2 ~ 1
  ),
  family = mixture(von_mises, von_mises, order = "none"),
  prior = prior(constant(0), class = Intercept, dpar = mu1) +
    prior(constant(0), class = Intercept, dpar = mu2) +
    prior(constant(-100), class = Intercept, dpar = kappa2) +
    prior(normal(2, 1), class = b, dpar = kappa1) +
    prior(logistic(0, 1), class = b, dpar = theta1) +
    prior(exponential(1), class = sd, dpar = kappa1) +
    prior(exponential(1), class = sd, dpar = theta1),
  data = dat,
  cores = 4,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "assets/brmsfit_brms_to_bmm"
)

kappa2 is fixed at -100 because brms estimates kappa on the log scale, and exp(-100) is as close to zero as anyone needs. At the default adapt_delta of 0.8, the sampler occasionally reports a divergent transition for this model, so we raise it; this is a brms argument and works the same in bmm(). file = saves the fit and loads it on later runs instead of refitting, so change the name, or drop the argument, when you change the data or the model. The last four priors are not the brms defaults. They are the priors bmm uses for this model, and we pass them here so that both fits are the same model. We come back to them in the section on priors.

2.3 The model in bmm

The bmm version needs a model object, one formula per parameter, and the data:

bmm_fit <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    kappa ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    thetat ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID)
  ),
  data = dat,
  model = mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error"),
  cores = 4,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "assets/bmmfit_brms_to_bmm"
)

The constraints are gone from the code. mixture2p() knows that the locations are 0, that the second component is the guessing distribution, and which priors to use. What is left is what you want to know: how kappa and thetat, the weight of the memory responses (the t stands for target), depend on set size.

2.4 Same model, same estimates

bmm translates its formula into a brmsformula, and brms writes the Stan model from that. You can look at the formula bmm generated:

bmm_fit$formula
#> response_error ~ 1 
#> mu1 ~ 1
#> kappa ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID)
#> thetat ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID)
#> kappa2 ~ 1
#> mu2 ~ 1
#> kappa1 ~ kappa
#> theta1 ~ thetat

kappa and thetat are non-linear parameters that bmm passes on to kappa1 and theta1. mu1, mu2 and kappa2 are fixed with constant priors, as in the brms call. Apart from the parameter names, the Stan code of the two fits is the same program with the same priors, so the posteriors agree up to the noise of the sampler. Both columns are on the link scale, log kappa and logit thetat, which we explain below:

brms_est <- fixef(brms_fit)
bmm_est <- fixef(bmm_fit)
ci <- function(est, row) {
  sprintf(
    "%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]",
    est[row, "Estimate"], est[row, "Q2.5"], est[row, "Q97.5"]
  )
}
set_sizes <- levels(dat$setsize)
comparison <- data.frame(
  parameter = rep(c("kappa", "thetat"), each = length(set_sizes)),
  set_size = rep(set_sizes, 2),
  brms = c(
    sapply(paste0("kappa1_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = brms_est),
    sapply(paste0("theta1_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = brms_est)
  ),
  bmm = c(
    sapply(paste0("kappa_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = bmm_est),
    sapply(paste0("thetat_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = bmm_est)
  )
)
knitr::kable(comparison, row.names = FALSE)
parameter set_size brms bmm
kappa 1 2.81 [2.69, 2.93] 2.81 [2.69, 2.92]
kappa 2 2.22 [2.10, 2.35] 2.23 [2.10, 2.35]
kappa 3 1.98 [1.82, 2.14] 1.99 [1.83, 2.14]
kappa 6 1.87 [1.58, 2.16] 1.87 [1.57, 2.15]
thetat 1 5.04 [4.13, 6.26] 5.06 [4.08, 6.32]
thetat 2 2.77 [2.28, 3.23] 2.77 [2.32, 3.22]
thetat 3 1.53 [1.11, 1.92] 1.54 [1.14, 1.90]
thetat 6 -0.60 [-1.02, -0.24] -0.59 [-0.99, -0.27]

For this model, bmm adds nothing to the Stan program. It writes the brms code, checks the data, and picks priors and starting values that suit the model. For models that brms has no family for, such as sdm() or cswald(), bmm also supplies the Stan code of the likelihood.

3 Where the response lives

In brms, the response is on the left-hand side of the main formula: response_error ~ 1. In bmm, it is an argument of the model object: mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error"). The formulas only ever have parameters on their left-hand side.

The reason is that a measurement model usually needs more than one column, and each column plays a different role. The three-parameter mixture model needs the response error, the colors of the items that were not cued, and the set size. A yes/no signal detection model fit to counts needs the number of “old” responses, the number of trials, and whether the item was old or new; with one row per trial, n_trials drops out. In brms, these roles end up spread over the response, addition terms such as | trials(), and predictors inside non-linear formulas. In bmm, the model object names each column once, by its role:

mixture3p(
  resp_error = "response_error", nt_features = "col_lure",
  set_size = "setsize", regex = TRUE
)
sdt_yn(response = "n_old", stimulus = "stimulus", n_trials = "n_trials")

Knowing the role of each column lets bmm check the data before anything is compiled. For instance, mixture2p() warns if the response error looks like degrees rather than radians. It also lets bmm build the columns that the Stan model needs from the ones you have, such as which of the non-target columns are filled at each set size. The help page of each model, such as ?mixture2p, lists the columns it expects.

4 Signal detection as a probit GLMM

A signal detection model can be fit without calling it that. With one row per trial, resp coded 1 for an “old” response and stimulus coded 1 for a studied item and 0 for a new one, a yes/no recognition experiment can be analyzed as a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a probit link:

brm(
  resp ~ 0 + Intercept + stimulus + (1 + stimulus | id) + (1 + stimulus | item),
  family = bernoulli("probit")
)

This is the equal-variance Gaussian signal detection model (DeCarlo 1998). In bmm, the same model is sdt_yn() with one row per trial: leave out n_trials, and response holds the 0 or 1 of each trial.

4.1 How the parameters map

The probability of an “old” response is pnorm(Intercept) for a new item and pnorm(Intercept + stimulus) for a studied one, where stimulus stands for its coefficient. In signal detection terms, these are pnorm(-criterion) and pnorm(d - criterion): the evidence of a new item is normal with mean 0 and standard deviation (SD) 1, that of a studied item normal with mean d, and the participant says “old” when the evidence lies above the criterion. The criterion is thus measured from the mean of the new items. Matching the two pairs of probabilities gives the intercept as minus the criterion and the stimulus coefficient as d. So each part of the brms model has a bmm name:

bmm (sdt_yn()) brms probit GLMM
d coefficient of stimulus
criterion minus the intercept
(1 \| id) in the formula of d stimulus slope by id
(1 \| id) in the formula of criterion intercept by id
(1 \| item) in the formula of d stimulus slope by item
(1 \| item) in the formula of criterion intercept by item
sdratio (unequal variance) none: the probit GLMM fixes both standard deviations at 1
bias (criterion measured from the midpoint between the two distributions) minus the intercept if stimulus is coded -0.5 / +0.5; with the 0 / 1 coding used here, -(Intercept + stimulus / 2)
dist (the distribution of the evidence) partly: bernoulli("logit") is dist = "logistic" and bernoulli("cloglog") is dist = "gumbel_max"; no link gives dist = "gumbel_min" for a response coded 1 = “old” (see below the table)

In the dist row, the link is that of the probability of an “old” response, whereas ?sdt_yn gives each dist by the cumulative distribution function of the evidence. The function 1 - exp(-exp(x)), the inverse of the complementary log-log link, is listed there under "gumbel_min"; the probability of “old” under "gumbel_max" is that same function of d - criterion. With the response coded 1 for “new” instead, bernoulli("cloglog") gives dist = "gumbel_min": the probability of “new” is that function of criterion - d * stimulus.

stimulus itself appears in no bmm formula: it is named in the model object, sdt_yn(stimulus = "stimulus"), and d is its effect, so a predictor in the formula of d is always one that interacts with stimulus. A predictor of the brms intercept is a predictor of criterion, with its sign flipped, and its interaction with stimulus is a predictor of d. For a design factor cond, resp ~ 0 + Intercept + stimulus * cond is bmf(d ~ 1 + cond, criterion ~ 1 + cond). The d coefficients are the stimulus and stimulus:cond coefficients, and the criterion coefficients are the intercept and cond coefficients, each multiplied by -1.

The intercept by participant changes sign along with the intercept, so its SD is the SD of the criterion. Beyond the parameters, bmm adds helpers for the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and the area under the ROC curve (AUC), which the signal detection article describes.

4.2 Both fits on one data set

To check the mapping, we simulate a recognition experiment in which 30 participants each see the same 60 items. Half of the participants studied items 1 to 30, the other half items 31 to 60, so every item is old for 15 participants and new for the other 15. d and criterion vary between participants and between items. The data come from the latent normal distributions of the model directly, not from a bmm function, so that the check does not depend on bmm’s own code:

set.seed(4646)
truth <- c(
  d = 1.3, criterion = 0.6,
  sd_id_d = 0.4, sd_id_criterion = 0.25,
  sd_item_d = 0.3, sd_item_criterion = 0.2
)
n_id <- 30
n_item <- 60
rec <- expand.grid(id = seq_len(n_id), item = seq_len(n_item))
rec$stimulus <- as.integer((rec$item <= n_item / 2) == (rec$id %% 2 == 1))

id_d <- rnorm(n_id, 0, truth[["sd_id_d"]])
id_criterion <- rnorm(n_id, 0, truth[["sd_id_criterion"]])
item_d <- rnorm(n_item, 0, truth[["sd_item_d"]])
item_criterion <- rnorm(n_item, 0, truth[["sd_item_criterion"]])
trial_d <- truth[["d"]] + id_d[rec$id] + item_d[rec$item]
trial_criterion <- truth[["criterion"]] + id_criterion[rec$id] +
  item_criterion[rec$item]

# new items draw their evidence from normal(0, 1), old items from normal(d, 1)
evidence <- rnorm(nrow(rec), mean = rec$stimulus * trial_d)
rec$resp <- as.integer(evidence > trial_criterion)
rec$id <- factor(rec$id)
rec$item <- factor(rec$item)
head(rec)
#>   id item stimulus resp
#> 1  1    1        1    0
#> 2  2    1        0    1
#> 3  3    1        1    0
#> 4  4    1        0    0
#> 5  5    1        1    1
#> 6  6    1        0    1

The brms fit is the GLMM from above. As in the first example, we give it the priors that bmm uses for sdt_yn(), so that the priors on the means and the SDs agree. ?sdt_yn lists them: normal(1, 1) on d, normal(0.5, 1.5) on criterion and exponential(1) on every SD. On the intercept, the criterion’s prior has its sign flipped:

glmm_fit <- brm(
  resp ~ 0 + Intercept + stimulus + (1 + stimulus | id) + (1 + stimulus | item),
  family = bernoulli("probit"),
  prior = prior(normal(-0.5, 1.5), class = b, coef = Intercept) +
    prior(normal(1, 1), class = b, coef = stimulus) +
    prior(exponential(1), class = sd),
  data = rec,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 646,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "fits/brmsfit_sdt_glmm_brms_to_bmm"
)

The bmm fit names the two columns in sdt_yn() and gives d and criterion a formula each:

trial_fit <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    d ~ 1 + (1 | id) + (1 | item),
    criterion ~ 1 + (1 | id) + (1 | item)
  ),
  data = rec,
  model = sdt_yn(response = "resp", stimulus = "stimulus"),
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 646,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "fits/bmmfit_sdt_trial_brms_to_bmm"
)

stimulus appears in neither formula. sdt_yn() reads it from the column named in the model object and uses it to decide whether d enters a trial, the job that the stimulus predictor does in brms. The 1 in d ~ 1 is the population d, the coefficient of stimulus in the GLMM, and (1 | id) lets it vary between participants, as the stimulus slope by id does.

The fits still differ in the correlations. (1 + stimulus | id) in brms also estimates the correlation between each participant’s intercept and slope, and the same for items. The bmm formula above leaves these correlations out. Write (1 + stimulus || id) to drop them in brms, or give the participant terms of d and criterion a shared ID, (1 | p | id), to add them in bmm. The bmm correlation is that of d and criterion, which is minus the brms correlation of slope and intercept, because the intercept is minus the criterion. The default priors on a correlation also differ: brms uses LKJ(1) and bmm uses LKJ(2): make_stancode() of the brms model shows LKJ(1), and stancode() of a bmm model with (1 | p | id) shows LKJ(2). prior(lkj(2), class = cor) gives the brms model the bmm prior.

The table puts the estimates of the two fits next to the values we simulated from, each as the posterior mean and its 95% credible interval (CrI). The brms intercept and its draws are multiplied by -1 to give the criterion:

glmm_draws <- as_draws_df(glmm_fit)
trial_draws <- as_draws_df(trial_fit)
glmm_par <- list(
  d = glmm_draws$b_stimulus,
  criterion = -glmm_draws$b_Intercept,
  sd_id_d = glmm_draws$sd_id__stimulus,
  sd_id_criterion = glmm_draws$sd_id__Intercept,
  sd_item_d = glmm_draws$sd_item__stimulus,
  sd_item_criterion = glmm_draws$sd_item__Intercept
)
trial_par <- list(
  d = trial_draws$b_d_Intercept,
  criterion = trial_draws$b_criterion_Intercept,
  sd_id_d = trial_draws$sd_id__d_Intercept,
  sd_id_criterion = trial_draws$sd_id__criterion_Intercept,
  sd_item_d = trial_draws$sd_item__d_Intercept,
  sd_item_criterion = trial_draws$sd_item__criterion_Intercept
)
mean_cri <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975))
  sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", mean(x), q[1], q[2])
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  parameter = c("d", "criterion", "SD of d by id", "SD of criterion by id",
                "SD of d by item", "SD of criterion by item"),
  `brms term` = c("stimulus", "-Intercept", "sd(stimulus) by id",
                  "sd(Intercept) by id", "sd(stimulus) by item",
                  "sd(Intercept) by item"),
  simulated = truth[names(glmm_par)],
  brms = vapply(glmm_par, mean_cri, character(1)),
  bmm = vapply(trial_par, mean_cri, character(1)),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE)
parameter brms term simulated brms bmm
d stimulus 1.30 1.24 [1.04, 1.45] 1.24 [1.05, 1.45]
criterion -Intercept 0.60 0.59 [0.45, 0.74] 0.59 [0.46, 0.72]
SD of d by id sd(stimulus) by id 0.40 0.37 [0.16, 0.59] 0.33 [0.16, 0.51]
SD of criterion by id sd(Intercept) by id 0.25 0.25 [0.09, 0.41] 0.23 [0.10, 0.36]
SD of d by item sd(stimulus) by item 0.30 0.27 [0.03, 0.49] 0.25 [0.04, 0.44]
SD of criterion by item sd(Intercept) by item 0.20 0.18 [0.03, 0.34] 0.16 [0.02, 0.28]

For every row, each fit’s estimate lies inside the other fit’s 95% CrI, and the two estimates differ by at most 0.04. Every simulated value lies inside both intervals. The intervals of the SDs are wide, because 30 participants and 60 items are few groups from which to estimate a spread.

4.3 The item effects on d

The item SD of d rests on fewer trials than the item SD of the criterion. On a trial with a new item, d does not enter the probability of an “old” response, pnorm(-criterion), so an item’s effect on d is estimated only from the trials on which the item was old: 15 per item here, against 30 for its effect on the criterion. The brms model says the same thing in its own terms: the stimulus slope by item multiplies a predictor that is 0 on every trial with a new item. In a design in which some items are never old, their effects on d stay at the prior. With bias instead of criterion, d also moves the criterion and enters every trial.

4.4 Aggregated counts

Item terms need trial rows, because counts summed over a participant’s items no longer say which item each response came from. The same holds for predictors that change from trial to trial. Without item terms or trial-level predictors, you do not need trial rows. sdt_yn() also takes one row per participant and stimulus type, with the number of “old” responses and the number of trials. This layout is faster, because the time a fit takes grows with the number of rows: here, 60 rows instead of 1800.

rec_counts <- aggregate(
  cbind(n_old = resp, n_trials = 1) ~ id + stimulus,
  data = rec, FUN = sum
)
agg_fit <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(d ~ 1 + (1 | id), criterion ~ 1 + (1 | id)),
  data = rec_counts,
  model = sdt_yn(response = "n_old", stimulus = "stimulus",
                 n_trials = "n_trials"),
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 646,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "fits/bmmfit_sdt_agg_brms_to_bmm"
)

For this model, the 1800 trials and the 60 counts give the same posterior, because the counts keep everything the trials say about the parameters. To check this, we take every posterior draw of agg_fit and compute two log-likelihoods: that of the 1800 trial rows, each written as a count of 0 or 1 out of 1 trial, and that of the 60 counts. Their difference, the gap, is printed as its range over all draws. If the gap is the same in every draw, the two log-likelihoods are the same function of the parameters up to a constant, and with the same priors they give the same posterior. The second line computes the constant we expect:

rec_single <- transform(rec, n_old = resp, n_trials = 1)
loglik_gap <- rowSums(log_lik(agg_fit, newdata = rec_single)) -
  rowSums(log_lik(agg_fit))
range(loglik_gap)
#> [1] -889.9357 -889.9357
-sum(lchoose(rec_counts$n_trials, rec_counts$n_old))
#> [1] -889.9357

The gap is the same in every draw, up to rounding, and equals minus the sum of the log binomial coefficients of the counts. That term does not depend on any parameter, so it drops out of the posterior.

4.5 Running and comparing trial-level fits

Trial-level fits take longer because they evaluate the likelihood of every trial. With backend = "cmdstanr", bmm(..., threads = threading(4)) evaluates it on four threads in each chain, which shortens the fit if your machine has cores to spare beyond the chains. threading() is the brms function that sets this up, and threads = 4 is short for it.

loo() on a trial-level fit leaves out one trial at a time; on the aggregated fit, it leaves out one count, that is, all trials of a participant and stimulus type at once. These are different predictions, so compare the loo() results only between fits to the same rows. To compare a trial-level fit with an aggregated one, use kfold(fit, group = "id"), which leaves out whole participants in either layout.

5 One formula per parameter

Because the response lives in the model object, a bmmformula is a list of regressions, one for each parameter of the model. Each one is a regular brms formula, with population-level effects, group-level effects in the lme4 syntax, and non-linear terms if you need them. The bmmformula article covers the syntax in full, including how to fix a parameter to a constant.

5.1 0 + setsize or 1 + setsize

Most bmm articles write 0 + setsize, and you may be used to 1 + setsize (or just setsize, which is the same thing). Both describe the same regression of each parameter on set size. They differ in what each coefficient means, and, as we show below, in which default prior each coefficient gets.

With 0 + setsize, the formula has no intercept, and there is one coefficient per set size. Each coefficient is the parameter in that cell of the design: kappa_setsize1 is kappa at set size 1, kappa_setsize6 is kappa at set size 6, both on the log scale explained below. This is often easier when you start out, because the summary shows the estimate for each condition directly, and those are the numbers you want to plot or report. If you are not sure which coding to use, start with this one.

With 1 + setsize, the intercept is the parameter in the reference condition, set size 1, and the other coefficients are differences from it. kappa_setsize6 is now how much log kappa at set size 6 differs from log kappa at set size 1. This coding is just as suitable, and it reads naturally when the difference between conditions is your question. To get the parameter in a cell, you add the coefficients:

bmm_fit_ref <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    kappa ~ 1 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    thetat ~ 1 + setsize + (1 | subID)
  ),
  data = dat,
  model = mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error"),
  cores = 4,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "assets/bmmfit_brms_to_bmm_reference"
)
fixef(bmm_fit_ref)[c("kappa_Intercept", "kappa_setsize6"), ]
#>                   Estimate  Est.Error      Q2.5      Q97.5
#> kappa_Intercept  2.8105353 0.06038921  2.694992  2.9271767
#> kappa_setsize6  -0.9254779 0.15041941 -1.222528 -0.6306745

draws_ref <- as_draws_df(bmm_fit_ref)
draws_cell <- as_draws_df(bmm_fit)
kappa6_ref <- draws_ref$b_kappa_Intercept + draws_ref$b_kappa_setsize6
kappa6_cell <- draws_cell$b_kappa_setsize6
rbind(
  `1 + setsize` = quantile(kappa6_ref, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  `0 + setsize` = quantile(kappa6_cell, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
)
#>                 2.5%      50%    97.5%
#> 1 + setsize 1.596731 1.883600 2.176051
#> 0 + setsize 1.570206 1.869862 2.153408

Add the coefficients draw by draw, as above, and summarize afterwards. The draws carry the uncertainty of each coefficient and how the coefficients covary, which adding the two point estimates loses. The reverse also works: a difference between set sizes is the difference of two cell coefficients of the 0 + setsize fit, again taken per draw.

Doing this by hand for every cell and parameter gets tedious. native_parameters() does it for you. It evaluates every parameter in every cell of the design, whatever the coding of the formula, and reports it on the scale of the model (more on scales in the next section). Here are both fits side by side:

np_cell <- native_parameters(bmm_fit, re_formula = NA, summary = TRUE)
np_ref <- native_parameters(bmm_fit_ref, re_formula = NA, summary = TRUE)
fmt <- function(np) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", np$Estimate, np$Q2.5, np$Q97.5)
np_cell <- np_cell[np_cell$parameter %in% c("kappa", "thetat"), ]
np_ref <- np_ref[np_ref$parameter %in% c("kappa", "thetat"), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  parameter = np_cell$parameter,
  set_size = np_cell$setsize,
  `0 + setsize` = fmt(np_cell),
  `1 + setsize` = fmt(np_ref[match(paste(np_cell$parameter, np_cell$setsize),
                                   paste(np_ref$parameter, np_ref$setsize)), ]),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE)
parameter set_size 0 + setsize 1 + setsize
kappa 1 16.63 [14.74, 18.60] 16.65 [14.81, 18.67]
kappa 2 9.28 [8.15, 10.53] 9.27 [8.09, 10.51]
kappa 3 7.31 [6.26, 8.49] 7.31 [6.26, 8.46]
kappa 6 6.54 [4.81, 8.61] 6.66 [4.94, 8.81]
thetat 1 0.99 [0.98, 1.00] 0.99 [0.98, 1.00]
thetat 2 0.94 [0.91, 0.96] 0.94 [0.91, 0.96]
thetat 3 0.82 [0.76, 0.87] 0.83 [0.76, 0.88]
thetat 6 0.36 [0.27, 0.43] 0.36 [0.28, 0.45]

Unlike the coefficients in the first table, these values are on the scale of the model: kappa is the precision itself, not its log, and thetat is shown as the probability of a memory response, not its logit. re_formula = NA sets the participant effects to zero, which gives the parameters of a typical participant; ?native_parameters explains how this differs from the population average under a non-identity link.

On the scale of the model, the two codings give practically the same estimates. In every cell, the estimates of the two fits differ by less than 1.8% of the 0 + setsize estimate; the largest gap is kappa at set size 6, 6.54 against 6.66. Pick the coding whose coefficients you want to read.

What the coding does change is the default prior of each coefficient. bmm sets its default priors per coefficient, and the value of a parameter in one cell is a different quantity from the difference between two cells: the first lies somewhere in the plausible range of the parameter, the second is centered on zero. With 0 + setsize, every coefficient is a cell, so every one gets the prior for the parameter itself, normal(2, 1) for kappa on the log scale and logistic(0, 1) for thetat. With 1 + setsize, only the intercept, the reference cell, gets that prior. The differences get the prior for effects, normal(0, 1) for kappa and normal(0, 2.5) for thetat. Any other cell is the intercept plus a difference, so its prior is that of a sum of two independent coefficients. For kappa, the two normal priors add up to normal(2, 1.41), whose standard deviation is the square root of 1² + 1²: wider than the normal(2, 1) that the same cell gets with 0 + setsize. With this data set, the table above shows that the difference barely matters. The table hides one exception, visible only on the logit scale: thetat at set size 1. Near a probability of 1, the data say little about the logit, and with 1 + setsize the effects prior, centered on zero, pulls the reference cell towards the other set sizes. On the logit scale, the two fits estimate thetat at set size 1 as 5.06 and 4.70, and the set-size differences of thetat differ by up to 0.42 logits. With fewer trials per cell, the priors carry more weight, and the two codings can give different estimates. So check default_prior() for the coding you use, as shown in the section on priors, and set your own priors if the defaults do not match what you know.

The participant effects can be coded either way, too. (1 | subID), as here, gives every participant one shift for all set sizes. (0 + setsize | subID) and (1 + setsize | subID) both let participants differ per set size, coded as cell values or as differences from the reference cell.

6 Which scale the estimates are on

The summary of a bmm fit lists the link of each parameter:

summary(bmm_fit)
  Model: mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error") 
  Links: mu1 = tan_half; kappa = log; thetat = logit 
Formula: mu1 = 0
         kappa ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID)
         thetat ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID) 
   Data: dat (Number of observations: 4000)
  Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
         total post-warmup draws = 4000

Multilevel Hyperparameters:
~subID (Number of levels: 8) 
                     Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
sd(kappa_Intercept)      0.09      0.06     0.01     0.23 1.01      675     1420
sd(thetat_Intercept)     0.39      0.16     0.17     0.77 1.00     1236     1794

Regression Coefficients:
                Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
kappa_setsize1      2.81      0.06     2.69     2.92 1.00     2722     2078
kappa_setsize2      2.23      0.07     2.10     2.35 1.00     2361     2233
kappa_setsize3      1.99      0.08     1.83     2.14 1.00     3120     2769
kappa_setsize6      1.87      0.15     1.57     2.15 1.00     2948     2364
thetat_setsize1     5.06      0.56     4.08     6.32 1.00     3247     2143
thetat_setsize2     2.77      0.23     2.32     3.22 1.00     2053     2104
thetat_setsize3     1.54      0.19     1.14     1.90 1.00     1648     1481
thetat_setsize6    -0.59      0.19    -0.99    -0.27 1.00     1602     1516

Constant Parameters:
                  Value
mu1_Intercept      0.00

Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

kappa must be positive, and thetat turns into a probability. Neither can be predicted by a linear model directly, so bmm estimates them on an unbounded scale and transforms them back. kappa has a log link, so the coefficients are log precisions. thetat has a logit link. brms fixes the weight of the second, guessing component (theta2) at 0 on this scale, so a thetat of 0 means that memory and guessing are equally likely, and the probability that a response comes from memory is plogis(thetat). Every coefficient in the summary, every prior, and every value you fix a parameter to lives on this link scale.

To report a parameter on its own scale, transform the draws and summarize afterwards, not the other way around. The mean of exp() of the draws is not exp() of their mean. For set size 6:

c(
  `exp(mean)` = exp(mean(kappa6_cell)),
  `mean(exp)` = mean(exp(kappa6_cell))
)
#> exp(mean) mean(exp) 
#>  6.475063  6.543754

native_parameters(), used above, follows this order for every parameter. For the mixture models, k2sd() converts kappa into the circular standard deviation in radians, which is the measure of precision many papers report:

kappa_draws <- native_parameters(bmm_fit, re_formula = NA, pars = "kappa")
sd_deg <- k2sd(kappa_draws$value) * 180 / pi
tapply(sd_deg, kappa_draws$setsize, median)
#>        1        2        3        6 
#> 14.27673 19.38314 22.02748 23.50076

A coefficient on its own transforms to something else. With 1 + setsize, exp(b_kappa_setsize6) is the factor by which kappa at set size 6 is larger or smaller than at set size 1, not kappa at set size 6. The help page of each model lists the links of its parameters.

7 Why the default priors are informative

brms uses flat priors on regression coefficients unless you set them. For the brms version of this model, the defaults are:

default_prior(
  bf(
    response_error ~ 1,
    kappa1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    theta1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    mu2 ~ 1,
    kappa2 ~ 1
  ),
  data = dat,
  family = mixture(von_mises, von_mises, order = "none")
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  transform(prior = ifelse(prior == "", "(flat)", prior)) |>
  subset(dpar %in% c("kappa1", "theta1") & coef == "" & group == "",
         select = c(dpar, class, prior)) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
dpar class prior
kappa1 b (flat)
kappa1 sd student_t(3, 0, 2.5)
theta1 b (flat)
theta1 sd student_t(3, 0, 2.5)

class = b covers every coefficient of kappa1 and theta1, so each of them has a flat prior. That suits a regression whose coefficients could take any value. It does not suit a measurement model. Its parameters stand for cognitive processes, and we know roughly which values are plausible before seeing any data. bmm puts this knowledge into its default priors:

default_prior(
  bmf(kappa ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID), thetat ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID)),
  data = dat,
  model = mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error")
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  subset(dpar %in% c("kappa", "thetat") & coef == "" & group == "",
         select = c(dpar, class, prior)) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
dpar class prior
kappa sd exponential(1)
kappa b normal(2, 1)
thetat sd exponential(1)
thetat b logistic(0, 1)

The normal(2, 1) on the log of kappa places 95% of its mass between a kappa of 1.0 and 52.5, that is, between a circular standard deviation of 71 and 8 degrees. Values in the thousands, which would mean a circular standard deviation of 1.8 degrees or less, get next to no prior mass. The logistic(0, 1) on thetat is flat on the probability scale: before seeing the data, every probability of a memory response between 0 and 1 is equally likely. It still does work that the brms default does not: a flat prior on the logit is improper and, on the probability scale, piles its mass at 0 and 1.

There is a second reason, which has to do with the mixture. When kappa comes close to 0, the memory distribution becomes as flat as the guessing distribution, and the data cannot tell the two apart. In that region, thetat can take any value without changing the fit. A flat prior does nothing to keep the sampler out of that region; a prior that holds kappa in a plausible range does.

What this means for you:

  • The more trials per participant and condition, the less the estimates depend on the priors. With few trials, the priors pull the estimates towards their center.
  • Look at the priors before you fit, with default_prior() as above, and at the help page of the model, which lists them.
  • If you know more than the defaults, or something different, set your own priors with prior = in bmm(). They are brms priors on the bmm parameter names, with nlpar or dpar as default_prior() shows it, for example prior(normal(1.5, 0.5), class = b, nlpar = kappa), again on the log scale. With 0 + setsize, this sets the prior of every cell of kappa. With 1 + setsize, it sets the prior of the differences only; the intercept takes coef = "Intercept", as default_prior() shows for that coding. The article on extracting model information shows the details.
  • Bayes factors depend on the priors much more than estimates do. If you plan to compute them, choose the priors on purpose rather than taking the defaults.

8 What stays brms

A bmm fit is a brmsfit with extra information, so the brms toolbox works on it: fixef(), ranef(), as_draws_df(), pp_check(), conditional_effects(), hypothesis(), loo() and the rest. As shown above, bmm_fit$formula holds the brmsformula that bmm generated, and stancode(bmm_fit) the Stan code. summary(bmm_fit, backend = "brms") prints the brms summary instead of the bmm one. It lists the link of theta1 as identity, because brms applies the softmax inside the mixture family. If you want to change a model beyond what bmm offers, these give you the brms code to start from.
